title: Attention Sees, MLP Refuses: Tracing the Attention-to-MLP Safety Pathway in LLMs
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Attention Sees, MLP Refuses: Tracing the Attention-to-MLP Safety Pathway in LLMs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. Across 18 Base-Instruct pairs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, particularly in early layers, whereas MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing in aligned models. Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs without systematically improving harmfulness decodability, while positive MLP writing becomes more concentrated in deeper layers after post-training. Across six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains decodable during reasoning while strong refusal writing concentrates at answer onset, a pattern that persists with reasoning disabled. Causal interventions further support this pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to their clean values substantially reduces the refusal shift caused by upstream attention interventions. Building on these findings, we introduce Sentinel, which combines an attention-derived perception score P with an MLP-derived decision score D. Their joint profiles characterize jailbreaks and over-refusals, and conditional routing with both signals achieves a lower aggregate error rate than single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.

report.summary: A new interpretability study shows attention layers detect harmful intent while MLP layers write refusals, yielding a dual-score Sentinel router that cuts jailbreak and over-refusal errors.
report.background: Safety-aligned LLMs are trained to refuse harmful requests, yet they remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and often over-refuse benign prompts. Prior interpretability work mostly locates 'safety features' somewhere in the residual stream without separating perception from action. This paper reframes the problem as a pathway: which module reads harmfulness, and which module writes the refusal? Using base-instruct model pairs across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma families, the authors measure residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, decoding harmfulness information from attention and MLP updates separately and tracking how post-training, reasoning mode, and causal interventions change each. The result is a mechanistic account of the attention-to-MLP safety pathway and a practical routing scheme built on it.
key_points: Attention updates expose harmfulness more clearly than MLP updates, especially in early layers, across 18 base-instruct model pairs. That suggests detection happens early and broadly.
MLP updates do the refusal writing: in aligned models, MLP changes are more harm-selective, meaning they translate recognized harm into readable refusal evidence.
Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs but does not systematically improve harmfulness decodability, so alignment mostly sharpens the response, not the perception.
In six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness stays decodable throughout reasoning, but strong refusal writing spikes at answer onset, a pattern that persists even when reasoning is disabled.
Causal tests show resetting downstream MLP updates to clean values largely cancels refusal shifts caused by upstream attention edits, supporting a directional attention-to-MLP pathway.
The Sentinel method combines an attention-based perception score P with an MLP-based decision score D; joint routing beats single-signal routing and fixed reminders across eight models.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this work shifts safety evaluation from 'does the model know it is harmful' to 'does the model act on that knowledge,' which could reshape alignment training, red-teaming, and content-moderation pipelines. Developers gain a mechanistic target: attention-side perception and MLP-side decision can be monitored, steered, or routed separately, potentially enabling cheaper jailbreak detection and over-refusal mitigation without retraining. Regular users could see models that refuse less often on harmless edge cases while still blocking genuinely dangerous requests, though dual-score routing also means safety behavior becomes a tunable knob rather than a fixed property. The findings also raise governance questions about whether perception and refusal can be audited independently.
report.tools: Sentinel is the paper's proposed dual-score router; watch for an official release. To reproduce or extend the work, use TransformerLens, nnsight, or Pyvene for residual-stream interventions, and SAELens for sparse-feature analysis. Hugging Face hosts Qwen, Llama, and Gemma checkpoints suitable for base-instruct comparisons. For causal tracing, consider circuit-tracer and standard activation-patching notebooks, plus LLM-as-judge harnesses for measuring over-refusal and jailbreak rates.
